title: BofA resets Dell stock price target by $100 after record earnings
detail:
BofA resets Dell stock price target by $100 after record earnings
Mwangi Enos, Celine Provini
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 2:03 PM EST 5 min read
DELL
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

I've learned that a stock can deliver impressive results and still struggle to move higher. Sometimes, the market is less interested in what a company has just achieved than in whether it can keep delivering at the same pace.

Dell Technologies (DELL) reported a record third quarter on Nov. 24, raised guidance, and still fell about 5% in early trading the following day. 

Seven of the eight firms that updated price targets lowered them, according to TheFly. Bank of America's Wamsi Mohan, ranked 26th out of 12,606 analysts on TipRanks with a 59% success rate, cut his target to $500 from $600 in a note shared with TheStreet, a 16.67% reduction.

His reasoning? "The market continues to question sustainability."

DELL is still up 129.34% year to date and 129.27% over one year as of Nov. 25, according to Yahoo Finance. This is despite recording an all-time high of $595.51 on Sept. 18, 2026, and currently trading 52% below the high.

The stock is not struggling. The question is how much growth is already in the price.

Also Read: Dell Technologies Q3 2027 Earnings: Recap of $DELL Earnings Call, Stock Forecast

Dell's tension: a great quarter, a lower multiple

Mohan said Dell delivered another strong quarter and outlook. What he changed was the valuation multiple he applies to Dell's earnings, citing risks to the AI infrastructure buildout and Dell's exposure to neoclouds. These newer AI-focused cloud providers have leaned heavily on debt to expand.

That worry has a backdrop. Piper Sandler pointed to the "sharp sell-off across AI and infrastructure names over the last two months, according to Stocktwits." 

More Tech:

Apple CEO signals surprising change for iPhone users

Comcast sends wake-up call to employees as customers cut services

AI agents' growing role in payments raises an awkward question

I covered the same fear when Oracle's credit spreads widened, and its bonds were questioned. The debate has moved from whether AI demand is real to who is financing it, and for how long.

Dell's answer came from COO Jeff Clarke on the earnings call: "We've had no customers reschedule business. The backlog continues to be very firm." He said the company remains "highly selective" with Neocloud customers and that every order is "rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power."

What the Dell quarter showed

According to Dell's earnings release, Q3 revenue was a record $54.9 billion, up 103%. Non-GAAP EPS was $9.45, up 265%. Cash flow from operations was a record $4.5 billion for a third quarter.

title: Bank of America issues blunt 2027 hard-landing warning on S&P 500
detail:
Bank of America issues blunt 2027 hard-landing warning on S&P 500
Moz Farooque, Aparajita Chatterjee
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 12:03 PM EST 5 min read
BAC
^GSPC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Judging from Wall Street's early 2027 stock market forecasts, it might seem that autumn's turbulence was more or less a brief speed bump. 

Major investment banks still continue to project another banner year ahead, even after Federal Reserve rate-hike jitters and AI spending doubts knocked the S&P 500 down from its Oct. 6 record of 7,818.93 to 7,201.09 on Nov. 24.

Bank of America Securities isn't buying that complacency though. In a note shared with me, Chief Investment Strategist Michael Hartnett issued a blunt reality check for investors heading into 2027.

Though most on Wall Street are calling for smooth sailing, Hartnett warns that a painful economic slowdown is perhaps the single biggest underpriced risk in markets today and is advising clients to play defense now.

Bank of America outlines a possible S&P 500 decline amid recession risks.
Spencer Platt / Getty Images
Inside Bank of America's 2027 S&P 500 forecast and hard-landing math

Hartnett's alarm starts off with a growing gap between market nerves and institutional positioning. 

As per Bank of America's November Global Fund Manager Survey as reported by Biggo, just 3% of fund managers are forecasting a steep downturn over the next 12 months, in comparison with 50% expecting a soft landing and 42% predicting no landing at all.

More Wall Street:

Arista Networks stock gets fresh backing from Jim Cramer and Wall Street

Oracle stock sinks as Wall Street confronts a $20 billion AI problem

Wall Street just got a candid look at who is winning the AI race

Cash levels have dropped to a historically thin 3.6%, down from 3.9% in October, even as global stock funds absorbed $310 billion over the past four weeks.

That crowding leaves stocks remarkably exposed. Hartnett warned that a "hard landing" is the biggest threat to market consensus, arguing that Wall Street projections of 15% to 20% global earnings growth are currently looking too optimistic as AI capital spending and K-shaped wealth effects taper off. 

In a true bust, he projects a bear market that drags the S&P 500 down to nearly 6,666, implying a 7.4% to 8% downside from late-November levels.

For clarity, recession isn't Bank of America's base case. 

Under a "Goldilocks" soft landing scenario that involves global growth above 3%, dropping inflation, sliding oil prices, and 21 global rate cuts in the back half of 2027, Hartnett expects a bull market to broaden out that could potentially carry the S&P 500 to around 7,777, an 8% increase from Nov. 24, yielding 4% to 8% upside for global stocks, with an extreme AI-boom surprise reaching 8,888.

That discipline echoes Bank of America's broader view.

Nutanix Inc (NASDAQ:NTNX) lost its "buy" rating at Bank of America, which downgraded the stock to "neutral" and cut its price target to $62 from $78, citing uncertainty over CEO succession.

CEO Rajiv Ramaswami plans to step down once a successor is appointed, and the bank cited strategy and execution risks in lowering its valuation multiple from six times estimated 2027 calendar-year sales to four times estimated 2028 sales.

Bank of America also revised its estimates following updated guidance from Nutanix, which expects its roughly 5-percentage-point first-quarter margin beat to provide little benefit over the rest of fiscal 2027.

Planned hiring and spending on AI, cloud-native products and data sovereignty offerings limit those gains, and the bank said the scale of investment needed to compete in AI remains unclear.

Learn more about Nutanix

Read more about Nutanix

Those spending plans come amid weaker customer metrics, with net revenue retention slipping to 105% and calculated bookings tied to remaining performance obligations falling about 2% year over year.

Fewer large deals closed, and the bank saw limited evidence that the company was fully benefiting from strong sales of standard servers, even though its revenue is tied to enterprise server core counts.

Bank of America sees external storage as Nutanix's clearest near-term growth opportunity, citing the quarter's largest deal using Dell Technologies Inc (NASDAQ:DELL) PowerFlex and the broader availability of NetApp support.

Support for existing storage arrays also helps customers migrate from VMware, which the bank sees as a longer-term opportunity, while a prolonged CEO search poses a more immediate risk.

Canadian banks have little room to miss, Bank of America warns Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

Canadian banks have little room for earnings disappointments at premium valuations, Bank of America said as it trimmed fourth-quarter earnings per share estimates.

Bank of America expects management updates to do little to change investor optimism, with investors watching for early signs of a pickup in domestic investment.

Canadian banks trade at 13.8 times estimated 2027 earnings, while Bank of America forecasts earnings per share growth of 10.8% in 2027, down from 19.4% in fiscal year 2026.

With earnings growth set to slow, the bank expects revisions to earnings estimates to be the main driver of share performance.

Bank of America cited slower capital markets activity, expected restructuring charges at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) (TSX:CM) and Royal Bank of Canada (TSX:RY), and higher credit costs, particularly at Bank of Nova Scotia (TSX:BNS), for its fourth-quarter cuts.

Despite those pressures, the bank forecasts average return on equity of 16.1% in 2027, up 0.8 percentage points, helped by loan repricing, excess capital and efficiency efforts.

Among Canadian banks, TD Bank remains Bank of America's top pick for its execution and scope for internal improvements, while CIBC stands out for its exposure to domestic investment.

Bank of America expects TD Bank and Royal Bank of Canada (TSX:RY) to reframe their return targets, while Bank of Montreal is expected to reiterate its 15% target for the end of fiscal year 2027.

The next tests of management's plans to improve returns include National Bank of Canada (TSX:NA) strategic update and CIBC's investor day.

Bank of America Corporation BAC is strengthening its international banking franchise through significant expansion in Switzerland, where it recently marked 75 years of operations. The bank's Swiss corporate banking client base has tripled since January 2024, with client numbers increasing nearly 30% year to date. Further, since the launch of its Swiss growth initiative in 2021, the local workforce has doubled, reflecting continued investments in its international business.

Bank of America is expanding its Swiss operations by strengthening Financial Institutions Group (FIG) coverage, broadening corporate banking capabilities and growing its middle-market offering. The bank's local business spans mergers and acquisitions (M&A) advisory, equity and debt capital markets, corporate banking and Global Markets.

BAC has advised on several significant transactions involving Swiss companies over the past 18 months, including deals involving Lonza, ABB, Nestlé, Galderma, DocMorris and Swisscom. The bank has also strengthened its capital markets presence by underwriting equity and debt offerings, including Galderma's secondary accelerated bookbuild and bond offerings for Swisscom, Nestlé and Novartis.

The expansion aligns with Bank of America's broader international middle-market strategy, which initially gained traction in Switzerland and has since expanded into the United Kingdom, Ireland, Italy and Germany. The initiative provides companies with access to financing, treasury, payments and foreign exchange solutions, strengthening the bank's ability to serve businesses across multiple markets. Continued investments in local teams and broader client coverage should help deepen corporate relationships, generate cross-border business opportunities and diversify revenue streams.

BAC's investment banking fees increased 14.6% year over year in the first nine months of 2026, reflecting a recovery in capital markets activity. Although third-quarter investment banking fees, excluding self-led deals, declined 11% year over year, the bank remains focused on strengthening its advisory and capital markets capabilities. Continued international expansion and a growing corporate client base could support future advisory mandates, financing transactions and fee income generation.

Over the past three months, shares of BAC have declined 20.6%, underperforming the industry's 15.4% decline.

title: JPMorgan Rethinks UK Investments: Will Higher Taxes Hurt Growth?
detail:
JPMorgan Rethinks UK Investments: Will Higher Taxes Hurt Growth?
Swayta Shah

JPM
GS
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

JPMorgan JPM is reportedly reconsidering its planned investments in the United Kingdom as higher banking taxes threaten to weigh on profitability. The bank is evaluating potential spending reductions at its Bournemouth operations center and approximately £5 billion Canary Wharf development in London. However, neither project is likely to be abandoned.

The development follows CEO Jamie Dimon's Nov. 20 remarks about offsetting the financial impact of higher taxes. The U.K. banking surcharge is set to double from 3% to 6% for 15 months, beginning January 2027. The measure could increase JPMorgan's tax bill by £120 million, affecting after-tax earnings and investment returns.

Potential spending reductions underscore the company's focus on disciplined capital allocation and expense management. Scaling back infrastructure investments could help preserve cash flows and moderate future operating costs. JPMorgan may also reassess the geographical allocation of incremental investments, prioritizing markets offering more attractive risk-adjusted returns.

However, significantly curtailing U.K. investments could pose challenges. London remains a major global financial hub, offering access to institutional clients, skilled professionals and international capital markets. Reduced spending could limit JPMorgan's ability to expand operational capacity and capitalize on emerging business opportunities in the region.

JPMorgan's diversified revenue streams and robust earnings generation provide flexibility to absorb incremental tax costs. While disciplined spending could cushion the financial impact, prolonged tax uncertainty and reduced infrastructure investments may constrain international expansion. Management's ability to balance expense optimization with strategic investments will remain crucial to sustaining long-term earnings growth and shareholder returns.

JPMorgan's Peers & Their Global Expansion Initiatives

Two key peers of JPM are Bank of America BAC and Goldman Sachs GS.

Bank of America is strengthening its international presence through strategic hiring and broader corporate banking coverage. Bank of America has doubled its corporate banking team across Europe, the Middle East and Africa, targeting 40% client growth in the region to capitalize on cross-border financing and advisory opportunities.

Goldman continues to strengthen its international operations through workforce expansion across key financial and technology hubs. Goldman added 142 employees to its European banking operations over the past year, while its Indian workforce exceeds 8,000, supporting global operational capabilities and business expansion.

Warren Buffett and dividends are an old love story that continues to this day, as Berkshire's latest 13F filing shows. The filing also reveals portfolio changes as CEO Greg Abel reshapes Berkshire's stock holdings after succeeding Buffett in January as the Omaha, Nebraska-based conglomerate's leader. Berkshire bought $2.37 billion worth of stocks in the third quarter and sold $2.79 billion. You can read about the fund's latest holdings here.

Dividend stocks continued to take center stage in the portfolio. Most of Berkshire's holdings are in companies that pay dividends, and many of them offer solid payouts. This has been an important part of Buffett's investment strategy over the years, and his successors at the firm appear to share that approach.

Analysts have long questioned why Berkshire Hathaway does not pay dividends to its own shareholders. Buffett has always been confident in his ability to put the company's capital to better use. He believes investing in businesses and other opportunities can generate better returns than distributing cash to shareholders. Even when he feels Berkshire cannot find attractive investment opportunities for its growing cash pile, he would rather return capital through share buybacks than dividends. In a 2018 interview with CNBC, Buffett explained his thinking: "Dividends have the implied promise that you keep paying them forever and not decrease them." He has also argued that repurchasing Berkshire's own shares can be more beneficial for shareholders.

Also read: 10 Best Tech Stocks That Pay Dividends

In a 2023 report, The Wall Street Journal cited Todd Finkle, a professor of entrepreneurship at Gonzaga University and author of a book about Buffett's career. Finkle summed up Buffett's approach by saying, "That's what he loves: dividends and buybacks."

Finkle noted that Buffett has been particularly good at identifying businesses that can withstand different economic cycles while continuing to increase their dividends. These investments have helped grow the value of Berkshire's stock portfolio over time while bringing in cash that the company can use to support its businesses, make acquisitions, and buy back its own shares. For Buffett, dividends aren't "the secret sauce, but they're part of it," Finkle said. Given this backdrop, we will take a look at how much in estimated dividends Berkshire is expected to receive this year from some of its biggest holdings. title: Bank Bond Losses Hit $486 Billion: How Exposed Is Bank of America?

Bank Bond Losses Hit $486 Billion: How Exposed Is Bank of America?

WFC
JPM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Bank of America BAC faces mounting pressure on its securities portfolio as elevated interest rates weigh on bond valuations. According to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation's Nov. 24 report, unrealized securities losses across U.S. banks surged 48.8% sequentially to $486 billion in the third quarter of 2026, highlighting persistent balance-sheet challenges.

BAC remains particularly exposed, given its substantial held-to-maturity ("HTM") securities portfolio, accumulated largely during the low-interest-rate environment. Its gross unrealized HTM securities losses increased 29.4% to $103.9 billion as of Sept. 30, 2026, from $80.3 billion at 2025-end. Although these losses do not directly affect earnings, they reflect significant deterioration in the market value of its investments.

Bank of America's exposure to longer-duration, lower-yielding securities limits its ability to capitalize on elevated interest rates. Selling these securities to reinvest proceeds at higher yields could crystallize losses, potentially hurting earnings and capital. Moreover, higher deposit costs alongside relatively low returns on legacy securities could restrict net interest margin expansion and weigh on profitability.

The substantial unrealized losses also reduce BAC's balance-sheet flexibility, particularly if unexpected liquidity needs arise. BAC's average global liquidity sources declined to $914 billion in the third quarter of 2026 from $975 billion in the fourth quarter of 2025. Nonetheless, its diversified deposit franchise, strong earnings generation and recurring securities cash flows mitigate the risk of forced asset sales.

Going forward, the gradual maturity of legacy securities should allow Bank of America to redeploy funds into potentially higher-yielding assets, supporting net interest income growth. While declining long-term yields could ease valuation pressures, persistently elevated rates may prolong balance-sheet constraints. Hence, disciplined portfolio repositioning, effective funding cost management and adequate liquidity will remain critical to BAC's profitability and financial flexibility.

How Do Bank of America's Peers Fare?

JPMorgan Chase JPM also faces securities valuation pressures stemming from elevated interest rates. As of Sept. 30, 2026, JPMorgan's HTM securities portfolio stood at $274.6 billion, up from $270.1 billion at 2025-end. Its available-for-sale ("AFS") securities portfolio increased to $547.2 billion.

However, JPMorgan's strong liquidity position provides considerable flexibility in managing interest rate risks. At the third-quarter end, JPM had approximately $1.5 trillion in liquidity sources, while its average deposits increased 8% year over year. Its diversified revenue streams and robust funding base should help mitigate the impact of securities valuation pressures.

Wells Fargo & Company WFC has been gradually reshaping its investment portfolio. At third-quarter end, Wells Fargo's HTM securities declined 10% year over year to $189.3 billion, while AFS securities increased 25% to $247.7 billion. Nonetheless, combined net unrealized losses on these portfolios increased from the figure at 2025-end, primarily reflecting interest rate movements.

Wells Fargo's declining HTM securities exposure and growing AFS portfolio could provide greater flexibility in balance-sheet management. However, persistent securities valuation pressures and potential increases in funding costs could temper the benefits of portfolio repositioning on NII growth.
